== Biography == Hugh Glasgow, son of [[Glasgow-551|John Glasgow]], was reportedly born in County Tyrone, Ireland, about 1706. He later settled in County Londonderry, where he worked as a weaver and married [[McCullough-1964|Margaret McCullough]].[[Glasgow-590|William Melanchthon Glasgow]], ''History of the Glasgow Family'', [https://www.wikitree.com/photo/pdf/Glasgow-590 digital copy attached to Glasgow-590]. === Family tradition === In the family history written by Hugh's second great-grandson, [[Glasgow-590|William Melanchthon Glasgow]], Hugh is described as follows:
''was born in the County Tyrone about 1706. He was a weaver by trade, and followed this vocation. A little circumstance in his life is recorded to show how trifling transactions may determine our future place of residence. When a young man he had an unavoidable difficulty with a neighbor which resulted in personal combat. Being a strong and agile youth, he severely punished his dishonest debtor, in consequence of which he fled from the community, and found a resting place in the County Londonderry.'' ''He was soon employed at his chosen vocation by a man by the name of McCullough. He immediately gained the confidence of his employer, for undoubtedly the young man was a good workman. The aged weaver, however little suspected that the young man was falling deparately in love with his charming daughter. But such was the case; and the sequel was that Hugh Glasgow and Margaret McCullough celebrated their marriage in 1733. To them were born in due time, three sons, John, Robert, and Hugh.''
Hugh and [[McCullough-1964|Margaret McCullough]] married in 1733 and had three known sons: * [[Glasgow-549|John Glasgow]] * [[Glasgow-550|Robert Glasgow]] * [[Glasgow-540|Hugh Glasgow]] === Tamlaght O'Crilly === The 1740 Protestant Householders' Returns for County Londonderry contain two entries for men named Hugh Glasgow in Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish, Barony of Loughinsholin.Bill Macafee, compiler, ''Protestant Householders' Returns (1740) for County Londonderry'', records 1195 and 1272, Hugh Glasgow, Loughinsholin Barony, Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish; [https://adamsfamilydna.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/1740-Protestant-Returns-Londonderry-County-Ireland.pdf PDF]. In a transcription preserving the parish sequence, one of the entries appears in the following order: * Hugh Glasgow * Hugh Allice * James McCullough William Murphy, transcriber, “Census (Partial) of Protestant Householders in Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish in 1740,” ''Ireland Genealogy Projects Archives'', [https://www.igp-web.com/IGPArchives/ire/derry/census/cens-prot-tamlaght-1740.html online transcription]. This fits the family account closely. Hugh is found in the correct county and parish only a few years after his reported marriage, and his name appears almost immediately beside that of James McCullough. Taken together, the date, location and McCullough connection make this the strongest candidate for the Hugh described in the family history. The second Hugh Glasgow entry may represent another member of the wider Glasgow family living in the same parish. === 1772 record === A notice published in the ''Belfast News-Letter'' in April 1772 names a Hugh Glasgow among the inhabitants of Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish who surrendered their arms to Henry Ellis of Inishrush.''Belfast News-Letter'', 14 April 1772, notice dated at Inishrush on 6 April 1772, naming Hugh Glasgow among inhabitants of Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish; transcript in “1770–1779: News transcripts for Kilrea & environs,” [https://arborealis.ca/records/newspapers/kilrea-news/1770-1779/ Arborealis]. The notice places a Hugh Glasgow in the same parish district more than thirty years after the 1740 return. This may have been Hugh himself, then about sixty-six years old, although his adult son [[Glasgow-540|Hugh Glasgow]] was also living by that time. The 1740 and 1772 records together show a continuing Glasgow presence in Tamlaght O'Crilly and support the family's association with the district. === Later family in America === The family history later follows the household of Hugh's younger son, [[Glasgow-540|Hugh Glasgow]], who married Sarah or Sallie Blair. That branch of the family emigrated to America in August 1796 and arrived at New Castle, Delaware. They lived for about five years near Little York in York County, Pennsylvania. In 1802 they moved briefly to Washington County and later settled in Deer Creek Township, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania. === Later account === A later online genealogical account preserves a similar version of the family tradition:
''My great-great-grandfather: Hugh,1 GLASGOW, b. 1724, was a native of the County of Tyrone, Ireland. When a young man he fell out with a neighbor, engaged in a personal combat in which he was the victor, but because of prosecution and the severe penalty, he fled to County of Derry. Being a weaver by trade, he found employment with one McCullough. He soon, however, fell in love with his host's charming daughter, [Wm. M. never mentions her given Name?] and they were happily married. To them was born three sons:'' ''#1.1. John,1 GLASGOW'' ''#1.2. Robert,1 GLASGOW, and'' ''#1.3. Hugh,2 GLASGOW, b. 1753 m. Sarah BLAIR, 5Ch.''
Undated Glasgow family genealogy formerly hosted by RootsWeb, [https://web.archive.org/web/20201003134102/https://sites.rootsweb.com/~iapage/families/glasgow/GLASGOW1.HTM archived copy at the Internet Archive]. == Research Notes == === Dates === The family history written by [[Glasgow-590|William Melanchthon Glasgow]] gives Hugh's birth as about 1706 and his marriage to [[McCullough-1964|Margaret McCullough]] as 1733. The later online account gives Hugh's birth as 1724. That date does not fit comfortably with the reported 1733 marriage and may be a transcription error or a date belonging to another member of the family. The accounts also differ over the birth year of the younger [[Glasgow-540|Hugh Glasgow]]. The later account gives 1753, while the family history gives an earlier date. === Identification === The entry beside James McCullough in the 1740 Tamlaght O'Crilly return is the strongest match for this Hugh because it agrees with the location, period and McCullough association recorded in the family history. The presence of a second Hugh Glasgow in the same return suggests that there was another adult of the name in the parish, perhaps a relative. Not to be confused with: * [[Glasgow-1503|Hugh Glasgow]] * [[Glasgow-1056|Hugh Glasgow]] * [[Glasgow-1067|Hew Glasgow]] Hugh may also have been related to [[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow]]. == Sources ==

== Biography ==
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}


'''Barbara Glasgow''' was born circa 1586, likely in Scotland.<ref name="BirthEst">This birth year is estimated based on the 1611 birth of her daughter Catharine, assuming Barbara was in her early-to-mid-twenties at the time, a common age for mothers in this era. This is a genealogical estimation only and is not based on a birth record.</ref> Her parentage and specific place of birth remain unknown.

Barbara emerges in the historical record through her connection to the Little family in Edinburgh, the capital city of Scotland. In the early 17th century, Edinburgh was a significant administrative and religious center. Barbara's only confirmed vital event documented so far is the birth and baptism of her daughter in 1611, recorded in the Edinburgh Parish register (Midlothian). The details are:<ref name="Catharine1611">"Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4N-CDX : 16 September 2021), Johne Little in entry for Catharine Little, 1611. Citing Edinburgh Parish, Edinburgh, Midlothian, Scotland. Details also corroborated by FindMyPast transcription.</ref>

* '''Child''': [[Little-6307|Catharine Little]] (Born: 9 Sep 1611, Baptised: 29 Sep 1611)
* '''Father''': [[Little-6308|Johne Little (abt.1580-aft.1612)]]
* '''Mother''': '''Barbara Glasgow'''

This baptism likely took place at one of the main churches serving Edinburgh parish at the time, such as the High Kirk (St Giles'), St Cuthbert's, or perhaps Canongate Kirk. No further information about Barbara, such as a marriage record to Johne Little or a death record, has yet been definitively linked to this profile.

=== Disambiguation: Contemporaries and Potential Conflation ===
Extreme caution is required when researching Barbara Glasgow in early 17th century Edinburgh and its surrounds, as several women shared this name. The Barbara Glasgow documented as mother to Catharine Little must be carefully distinguished from other known individuals, including:

* '''Barbara Glasgow, wife of George Johnstoun:''' (Likely [[Glasgow-3302|Barbara (Glasgow) Johnson (abt.1600–)]]). FamilySearch profile 9VM1-52D appears to '''conflate''' this woman's records with the mother of Catharine Little. Records associated with this Barbara include:
** Marriage to George Johnstoun on 21 November 1616 in Edinburgh Parish.<ref name="JohnstounMarriage1616">"Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYMH-HZJ : 11 February 2020), Barbara Glasgow in entry for George Johnstoun, 1616.</ref>
** Several children christened in Edinburgh Parish with George Johnstoun between 1617 and 1627, including Daniell (1617)<ref name="Daniell1617">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YQ-BX4 : 16 September 2021), Barbara Glasgow in entry for Daniell Johnestoun, 1617.</ref> and Archebald (1618).<ref name="Archebald1618">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1Y3-2XL : 16 September 2021), Barbara Glasgow in entry for Archebald Johnstoun, 1618.</ref> (Other children mentioned in the source list for FS profile 9VM1-52D include Marione, Margaret, James, and Catharine Johnstoun).
** The estimated birth year of c. 1596 associated with FS profile 9VM1-52D fits this Barbara (wife of George Johnstoun) better than it fits the mother of Catharine Little.

* '''[[Glasgow-3182|Barbara (Glasgow) Wilson (abt.1590–)]]:''' Married [[Wilson-126696|John Wilson (1590–)]] on 26 November 1611 in South Leith Parish, Midlothian (adjacent to Edinburgh).<ref name="WilsonMarriage1611"> "Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYML-ZBB : 11 February 2020), Barbara Glasgow in entry for John Wilson, 1611.</ref>

* '''[[Glasgow-1102|Barbara Glasgow (1617-)]]:''' Baptised 29 June 1617 in Edinburgh Parish, daughter of George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart.<ref name="Barbara1617">"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQC9-JYX : 12 February 2020), Barbara Glasgow, 1617.</ref>

Given these contemporaries, it is crucial that further research confirms any additional records genuinely belong to the Barbara Glasgow who was mother to Catharine Little in 1611.

=== Research Notes ===

* '''Defining Record:''' This profile represents the Barbara Glasgow named as mother to Catharine Little, born 9 Sep 1611 and baptised 29 Sep 1611, daughter of Johne Little.<ref name="Catharine1611"/>
* '''Conflation Alert:''' FamilySearch profile 9VM1-52D appears to conflate this Barbara with Barbara Glasgow, wife of George Johnstoun (married 1616). Records require careful separation.
* '''Multiple Contemporaries:''' At least three, possibly four, women named Barbara Glasgow were living/marrying/having children in the Edinburgh/Leith area between 1610-1620, complicating identification.
* '''Conflicting Birth Estimates:''' The speculative birth estimate of c. 1586 fits better for the mother of Catharine Little (age ~25 in 1611). The FS profile estimate of c. 1596 fits better for the wife of George Johnstoun (age ~20 at marriage in 1616).
* '''Parentage & Origin Unknown:''' No sources confirming parents, specific origin, marriage, or death for Barbara (Glasgow) Little have been identified.

== Biography ==

John Glasgow was born in Ireland on 10 April 1767.<ref name="JohnRegister">[https://hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1 John Glasgow family register and descendant page] (accessed 20 July 2026).</ref><ref name="JohnLetter">[https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/documents/John%20Glasgow%20letter%20to%20Jane%20Glasgow%20Gray%203-20-1847.pdf John Glasgow to Jane Glasgow Gray, 20 March 1847], scan and transcript (accessed 20 July 2026).</ref> He married [[Arthur-2480|Mary Arthur]] on 21 May 1798, and their nine children were born in Ireland between 1799 and 1815.<ref name="JohnRegister" />

The family lived at '''Inishrush, County Londonderry'''. In 1847, John recalled that they had kept more bees there than they ever kept at one time after leaving Ireland.<ref name="JohnLetter" />

The first secure evidence of John in Ohio is his 1833 purchase of land in Guernsey County.<ref name="Deed1833">[http://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-89WY-TFPB Guernsey County deeds, volume H, page 457].</ref> He was recorded there in 1840.<ref name="Census1840">“'''United States Census, 1840''',” database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XHRF-1B6 : 8 September 2017), John Glascow, Guernsey, Ohio, United States; citing p. 355, NARA microfilm publication M704, roll 396; FHL microfilm 20,165.</ref> By 1847, John and Mary were being cared for by their son Arthur, who left “nothing undone” to make them comfortable.<ref name="JohnLetter" /> They were living in Arthur's household in Londonderry Township in 1850.<ref name="Census1850">“'''United States Census, 1850''',” database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MX3M-HP3 : 12 April 2016), John Glasgow in household of Arthur Glasgow, Londonderry, Guernsey, Ohio, United States; citing family 1538, NARA microfilm publication M432.</ref>

The Glasgows were a strict Covenanter family; family tradition states that even whistling on the Sabbath was forbidden.<ref name="JohnRegister" /> John's surviving letter reflects this outlook through repeated references to prayer, salvation and holding to Christ “for righteousness and life.”<ref name="JohnLetter" />

John died on 23 December 1851 and was buried in the Scotch Covenanter Cemetery in Guernsey County.<ref name="Grave">“Find A Grave Index,” database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVKX-FB2D : 13 December 2015), John Glasgow, died 1851; burial in Scotch Covenanter Cemetery, Guernsey County, Ohio; citing {{FindAGrave|43524841}}.</ref>

== Children ==

The Glasgow family register records nine children:<ref name="JohnRegister" />

* [[Glasgow-821|Rose or “Rosanna”]], born 4 March 1799; married Alexander McKeown in Ireland and settled in Harrison County, Ohio.
* '''[[Glasgow-3928|Maria ]]''', born 22 September 1800.
* '''[[Glasgow-3929|Jane]]''', born 5 October 1802; married John Gray in Ireland and settled in Kentucky. John's 1847 letter was apparently addressed to her.<ref name="JohnLetter" />
* [[Glasgow-3373|Adam]], born 7 July 1804.
* '''[[Glasgow-3930|Lavinia]]''', born 21 June 1806.
* [[Glasgow-1165|James]], born 9 November 1808; died 20 April 1823.
* [[Glasgow-43|Margaret]], born 17 October 1810; married John H. Walkinshaw.
* [[Glasgow-1617|John]], born 4 March 1813; died 17 August 1836 in Ohio.
* [[Glasgow-1608|Arthur]], born 1 July 1815; married Jane Neil.

== Research Notes ==

* [[Glasgow-3927|John Glasgow (bef.1813-)]] represents the John Glasco who headed house 2 at Inishrush in the 1831 census. His household contained four males and four females, all Presbyterian.<ref name="Census1831">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html “Tamlaght O'Crilly Census – 1831”], entry 1019, John Glasco, Innisrush house 2; transcription by Richard John Torrens (accessed 20 July 2026).</ref> The location, religion and household composition are compatible with this family, but the census gives no ages, names or relationships. If they were the same man, John emigrated between the 1831 census and his 1833 Ohio land purchase.<ref name="Census1831" /><ref name="Deed1833" />
* The John Glasgow recorded in Richland Township, Belmont County, in 1830 was aged forty to forty-nine and was almost certainly a different man. John, born in 1767, would have been about sixty-three. The citation is retained to document the rejected identification, but should not be used as evidence that he was in Ohio by 1830.<ref name="Ohio1830">[https://archive.org/details/populationsc18300127unit/page/n484/mode/1up 1830 United States census, Richland Township, Ohio], original census image (accessed 20 July 2026).</ref>

== Biography ==
=== Alexander’s life in its local setting ===

Alexander’s records describe a family rooted in a small part of County Antrim, with children whose later lives lead beyond it. His clearest surviving household is at Lisnagaver in 1851: an Antrim-born farmer, his wife Mary, and three children. Earlier baptisms recover the beginnings of that family; later marriages and the Elder tenancy connect it to the next generation. The probable Gortahar death completes the broad outline, with the last identity link still open.



==== The places in his life ====


Gortereghy<ref name="Evidencec9d92bcd01">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin-upper/gortereghy/ Gortereghy].</ref>, written Gortereagh in the baptism transcription, adjoins Lisnagaver<ref name="Evidence7d988f87c8">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/lisnagaver/ Lisnagaver].</ref> to the south. Gortahar<ref name="Evidence10a9c7be48">[https://www.townlands.ie/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/gortahar/ Gortahar].</ref> lies northeast, beyond Moneyleck. They are distinct townlands within the same parish. The map shows approximate modern townland locations, not reconstructed houses or field boundaries.


Both spouses reported first marriage in 1836. Their children’s baptisms place them at Gortereagh in 1837–38 and Lisnagaver by 1843. That suggests a change in the family’s recorded residence between neighbouring townlands; it does not date a move precisely or establish a return to a paternal home. Mary’s possible local family connections deserve investigation in their own right.


The census’s farmer and literate household, the small assessed tenancy and the children’s marriages recover part of Alexander’s circumstances. Later records call him a labourer, and his son-in-law succeeds him on the holding. These changes are compatible with an altered working role as he aged, but their cause is unknown. No inspected source establishes eviction, poverty, or illness-induced retirement. The record sequence and farm analysis distinguish those observations from assumptions about his life.


The following account traces marriage and children, examines the surviving household, then follows the farm, probable death and paternal connections. Missing parentage is one question within that family history.



=== Marriage, Mary’s family and the children ===

Alexander Glasgow and Mary/Molly McCaughan are a documented couple. Their 1851 household reports first marriage in 1836, but no original marriage entry has been located. Rasharkin Presbyterian’s surviving marriage register begins in 1845; First Kilraughts material (Coleraine Family History Society film 197, marriages from 1831) remains a focused alternative.


The marriage-year statement fits the first directly located record sequence. The published transcription of the original Rasharkin Presbyterian register, PRONI MIC1P/292, records the same parental couple at Gortereagh: James Glascaw was born 17 January and baptised 9 February 1837 to Alex and Mary McAughin; an incomplete 1838 entry records a Glascow child of Alex and Molly McAughern; and a later James Glascow was born 9 October 1843 and baptised 7 January 1844 to Alex and Molly McAughern at Lisnagaver. The named transcription can be checked at Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms].</ref>. The register transcription preserves Mary/Molly and McAughin/McAughern. The repeated parental names and residences support their identification with Mary McCaughan while retaining the spellings actually recorded.


The Gortereagh residence is meaningful maternal context, but it is not a parentage proof. The 1834 tithe list includes William and James McCaheran there, a spelling compatible with the recorded McAughin/McAughern/McCaughan forms. This makes a McCaughan family connection a reasonable explanation to test for the newly married couple’s residence, perhaps through Mary's people or a subtenancy. It does not prove that either man was Mary's father, nor that the first son James was named for a maternal grandfather. The 1851 Lisnagaver evidence supplies a more concrete lead: Mary McCaheren, 22, lived with farmer Archibald McCaheren, 60, and Elizabeth in house 31. She is the strongest currently located candidate for the later 1855 bride who named her father as Archy, but that is a separate McCaughan problem. It does not establish Mary Glasgow’s parentage. Likewise, the household of widowed Sarah McCaghrin and grandchildren beside widowed Margaret Elder and children is evidence of a local network of families and neighbours, not an expressed kinship.


The Gortereagh names are recorded in the 1834 Rasharkin tithe book, PRONI '''FIN/5/A/236'''; the 1851 McCaheren and Elder groupings are in Lisnagaver houses 31 and 5. These are separate record observations, not confirmed maternal relatives. See the National Archives census collection<ref name="Evidence0b09d5bb14">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/ National Archives census collection].</ref> and PRONI tithe-book guide<ref name="Evidenceb39783b2e9">[https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/tithe-applotment-books PRONI tithe-book guide].</ref>.

An authenticated FamilySearch search adds a useful comparison lead: a John McCaughan marriage at Rasharkin on 18 March 1851 names '''Jas McCaughan''' as his father, while a separate 1836 Lisnagaver valuation entry names '''Archibald Mccaughan Junr'''. The same search returns Archey and John McCaheran in the 1822–1840 tithe collection. These entries strengthen the conclusion that several similarly named families occupied the area, but their original images and townlands still need checking; none currently proves Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceFamilySearchMcCaughan">[https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/record/results?count=100&q.anyPlace=Rasharkin&q.surname=McCaughan FamilySearch Rasharkin McCaughan search], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>

A separate public Geneanet tree repeats the John McCaughern–Sarah Dysart marriage and proposes a 1872 death for John and a daughter, Mary Anne Jane Rea McCaughern, at Crushybracken about 1858. ==== What the gaps mean ====


The early children are documented separately from their inferred deaths. The table’s reuse-of-name argument does not supply an exact death date. Nor does the incomplete 1838 transcription identify its child as Samuel: an original copy of '''MIC1P/292, entry 106''' is needed to read the missing name and dates.


The transcription has no entries for 1840 or 1841, around Robert’s likely birth. Failure to find his baptism in that transcription is therefore weak evidence against the known parentage: the census and marriage positively establish his father. The missing original marriage, incomplete baptism entry and missing burial records are different gaps and need different searches.


The unnamed child would have been about twelve or thirteen in 1851. No resident, absent-person or household-death entry records that child in the maintained return audit. That omission weighs against an uncomplicated survival-and-emigration reconstruction, but cannot fix a death date or guarantee that the return was complete. The candidate Samuel Glasgow in Michigan was rejected because no American record supplied the required Antrim/parent bridge and the proposal also had to explain this omission. An impossible February date in a later cemetery transcription cannot name the child. The [[Glasgow-3940|child’s assessment]] preserves the comparison.



=== New parentage research: Mary’s McCaughan/McAughern network ===

The current evidence still does '''not''' prove the parents of [[McCaughan-222|Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow]]. The new research separates several local families that had previously risked being merged by surname and locality alone.

* The complete 1851 Rasharkin-derived return contains several relevant households: the older Archibald McCaheren family at Lisnagaver; William McCaheren; Sarah McCaghrin; Mary McCaheren, age 70, recorded as mother-in-law in the John and Margaret Taylor household; and an 11-year-old John McCaughern recorded as a servant/apprentice. None identifies Mary Glasgow, born about 1811, or names her parents.
* The Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription shows distinct McAughern/McAughin households: Eliza McAughern with Thomas at Carnfinton; Archy McAughern with Elizabeth Kilpatrick at Lisnagaver; and James McAughern, son of John and Jane McAuly, at Ballydonly. These records establish a local network, not a single extended family.
* The 1834 tithe material adds Alexr. McCaughan at Unchenagh in Finvoy, while the Drumadarragh family reconstruction identifies John McCaughey/McCahan, farmer, with children including Jane, Margaret, Nancy, James and Sarah. The Gortereghy William and James McCaheran group remains another candidate cluster. None is linked directly to Mary Glasgow.
* A separate National Archives census-search-form result documents Thomas McCaughern/McCaughan of Gortahar with father John McCaughern and mother Mary Gormley. This is a later-generation, parent-documented local family and does not prove Mary’s parentage.
* Authenticated FamilySearch searches for Mary McCaughan, McAughin, McAughern and McCaheren in the relevant Antrim period returned no indexed result. The apparent Alexander–Mary McCaughan hits belong to a different Catholic Culfeightrin/Ballycastle family, including Mary M’caughan’s 7 April 1867 baptism to Alex M’caughan and Cath Quinn. A separate Mary McCaughern–William Marks cluster is also later and unrelated.

The strongest new route is the pre-1831 '''Kilraughts–Dervock Reformed Presbyterian society material''', PRONI '''CR5/32A/1''' (also appearing in related catalogue references as '''CR5/32/1/1/1–2'''). The PRONI guide describes member-by-society lists, baptisms, marriages, deaths, removals and emigrations from about 1804–1831. Since Mary was probably born about 1811, a household or society entry could name her parents. The Kilraughts and Dervock societies operated together until their 1831 division, so both localities must be searched. This manuscript has not yet been inspected; it is a high-priority evidence target, not proof.

'''Current conclusion:''' Mary’s parents remain unknown. The local McCaughan/McAughern network is now better defined, and the Kilraughts–Dervock family lists are the highest-value unresolved route. No parent should be added to Mary’s profile until an original record explicitly connects her to a named household or parent couple.

=== Following the children into adult life ===


==== Robert: the recorded son and the Scottish continuation ====


Robert, aged ten in 1851, is directly recorded as Alexander and Mary’s son in the same Lisnagaver household. His 5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham<ref name="Evidence05c8c53b0b">[https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1866/11531/8240963.pdf 5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham].</ref> independently calls him a Lisnagaver farmer and names his father Alexander Glasgow, farmer. Those two records make Robert Glasgow-938 the documented child, with estimated birth about 1840–41 from the census and marriage ages. The often repeated exact 6 November 1840 birth date has no identified supporting original. His probable identification with a later Gortereghy valuation occupier is useful local continuity, but that identification is separate from the proved father–son relationship.


Robert’s later family is followed into Glasgow, Scotland, in the maintained account, which cites a 1871 Scottish census index for Robert<ref name="Evidencea991c3602f">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QV9Y-71S6 1871 Scottish census index for Robert].</ref> and an 1881 index for the younger Alexander<ref name="Evidencecfab144f27">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQQ8-5MB 1881 index for the younger Alexander].</ref>. [[Glasgow-937|Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-937)]], born about 1871, is the next historical generation in that family reconstruction. The Irish census and marriage provide the direct father–son argument for Alexander-951 and Robert; the Scottish continuation relies here on the maintained census references, not newly inspected original images. The copied exact birth date for the younger Alexander had been cited to the same index used for the census, so it is not adopted as an independently verified birth in this account. Exact Scottish address chronology and Robert’s reported 1902 death remain checks on their own originals.


This carries the story beyond the Antrim farm without making every copied detail equally secure. The tested descendant’s confirmed paternal ancestry reaches Alexander-951; the Y-DNA section explains the genetic comparison without listing living generations.


The precise Scottish birth-image leads and the misplaced 1902 death citation are assessed in the next research tests. Neither has yet been inspected; the direct Irish father–son evidence remains secure.



==== James: a strong Michigan candidate, still an open identity ====


The second James, Glasgow-973, has an unusually clear Irish identity: the 1843–44 baptism and his age seven appearance in the 1851 household establish him as Alexander and Mary’s child. His subsequent association with the James Glasgow buried at Tecumseh, Michigan is strong but still unproved. The Michigan household is well reconstructed: the original 1884 Michigan census image<ref name="Evidence13cf3f6b80">[https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_eb4d3f94-3c2f-4701-b5bb-c3ecee9ef9b9/ the original 1884 Michigan census image].</ref> gives a forty-year-old Irish-born baggage agent, and the Brookside register identifies the associated wife and daughters. His daughter Minnie’s 1941 death certificate<ref name="Evidence8b5b1f0905">[https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_3dab599e-1093-473c-be85-eee5e9b49154/ 1941 death certificate].</ref> reports James as born in County Antrim. That narrows the comparison materially but names neither Alexander nor Mary and gives no Lisnagaver detail. The 1869 original marriage return, naturalisation papers, or a passenger record is still required before the Michigan life becomes Alexander’s son’s biography.



==== Ann: a later marriage and the Nancy problem ====


Ann, Glasgow-438, is likewise direct family evidence. She was aged four in 1851 and her 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken<ref name="Evidence157ee58a9a">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1876/11181/8097170.pdf 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken].</ref> calls her a full-age spinster of Lisnagaver and names Alexander Glasgow, labourer, as father. The occupational wording matters because it independently makes the 1888 Gortahar death’s “labourer” compatible with the former Lisnagaver farmer; it is not grounds to split the two men. Ann’s later married surname also means Nancy Glasgow, who reported Alexander’s 1888 death, cannot simply be equated with her. A separate daughter, or another explanation, remains possible.



==== Mary: the daughter whose records connect the households ====


Mary Glasgow-3167 is not in the 1851 return but is securely added by her 14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder<ref name="Evidence5782477e56">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf 14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder].</ref>: aged 28, resident Lisnagaver, she named Alexander Glasgow, farmer, as father. Her marriage, Robert Elder’s succession to lot 25, and the Gortahar deaths create the high-confidence bridge between the Lisnagaver couple and Mary McCaughan’s later identity. Mary Glasgow’s 17 February 1892 death return<ref name="Evidence6f1ed437a9">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf 17 February 1892 death return].</ref> records daughter Mary Elder as informant. It does not state a maiden surname or husband, and its reported age 89 conflicts with the retained c.1811 estimate; those limits belong beside the identification, not beneath it.


Mary’s later household also contains an instructive name conflict. Her granddaughter’s 1908 birth<ref name="Evidencebe365902e1">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1908/01647/1657700.pdf 1908 birth].</ref> records '''Samuel Elder''', son of Jane Elder, with no father named; the 1911 household<ref name="Evidenceb4f7bd3ba5">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911 1911 household].</ref> calls him '''Samuel Glasgow'''. The surname is genuinely present in the census, not merely a modern transcription mistake. These records help reconstruct the continuing family, but neither identifies his father. It would be circular to invent a Glasgow father and then use that invented relationship to strengthen Alexander’s ancestry.


Mary’s absence in 1851 is consequently an unresolved location question within a well-supported later family identification. It does not erase the 1871 father statement. Nor does it establish that she was the Maryan in John of Glenleslie’s household: the roughly nine-year conflict between their implied birth years requires explanation, and no located record joins those two identities.

==== The identity chain, in dependency order ====


# The 1851 Lisnagaver house-35 return<ref name="Evidence96bd10f1c0" /> establishes Alexander and wife Mary, both reported aged 40, with children Robert, James and Ann. This is the starting household; its identity does not depend on either Gortahar death.
# Mary Glasgow’s 14 June 1871 marriage<ref name="Evidence5782477e56" /> identifies a 28-year-old Lisnagaver spinster, daughter of Alexander Glasgow, farmer, marrying Robert Elder, 40, farmer of Gortereghy. It directly establishes the bride’s father. Linking that father to the established Lisnagaver household uses name, residence and occupation; the marriage does not name her mother.
# PRONI valuation revisions<ref name="Evidence5c88fa9a83" />, VAL/12/B/4/16C–D, follow Alexander’s removal from '''Lisnagaver lot 25''' and Robert Elder’s subsequent occupation. Succession to the particular holding strengthens the identification of Robert with the daughter’s husband. The book neither declares an inheritance nor records Alexander’s destination or exact death. It supplies a separate administrative connection, not another explicit statement of kinship.
# The 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder<ref name="Evidence5aecbbb88b">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1878/02945/2078820.pdf 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder].</ref> places Robert Elder and Mary, maiden surname '''Glass''', at Gortahar. That named relationship supplies the strongest connection between the elderly Glasgow woman and the Elder family. With the preceding marriage and household evidence, it supports the high-confidence identification of the widow as [[McCaughan-222|Mary McCaughan (McCaughan-222)]]. It does '''not''' name her deceased husband.

The maintained comparison gives '''genetic distance three at Y-111''' between the Alexander and James J descendant lines. That makes their connection a valuable research priority. FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance<ref name="Evidencee3eb9bbee5">[https://blog.familytreedna.com/ftdnatip-report/ FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance].</ref>.


Another Glasgow line is closer on the larger callable Big Y STR comparison. The inspected August 2026 Block Tree contains no exclusive named downstream branch joining only these two lines. Wider Y-DNA study and comparison evidence.


Brothers, paternal cousins and descendants of more distant collateral branches remain distinguishable historical hypotheses; the present DNA cannot choose among them. Their similar estimated birth years do not locate their common ancestor. A connection through an earlier generation, followed by migration in one branch, remains compatible with the results. A specific migration route is not established. An exact ancestor, date or cousin degree requires evidence connecting the named people, supported where possible by additional independent descendant comparisons.

=== The wider family: proved links and open bridges ===

The Lisnagaver evidence supports a local Glasgow network; it does not yet yield a single reconstructed pedigree. The starting point is the 1851 sequence. House 34<ref name="Evidence2c97cf113b" /> contains John Glasgow, farmer, with wife Margaret and his unmarried brother Samuel, a linen weaver. House 35<ref name="Evidencedea66e5c28" /> contains Alexander and Mary with their children. House 37<ref name="Evidence6c8cd27a9f" /> contains Thomas Glasgow and Mary Ann. A Watters household separates Alexander and Thomas. The layout establishes a small same-surname farming cluster and useful geographic proximity; enumeration order is not a kinship statement or a property map.


John Glasgow-867 and Samuel Glasgow-2908 belong to a specific '''father-John branch'''. John’s original 16 November 1846 marriage<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063 original 16 November 1846 marriage].</ref> names his father as John Glasgow, farmer. The 1851 household expressly calls Samuel John’s brother. That chain directly establishes the brotherhood and names John-867’s father and his occupation. Extending that father statement to Samuel assumes they shared a father; the census does not distinguish full from half brothers. It does '''not''' identify that father with John Glasgow-1022, the older Glenleslie man, and it does not make Alexander another son. The younger John’s memorial says he died in 1895 aged 78, which implies a birth about 1816–17 and makes the candidate Glasgow-1022 less comfortable than an earlier census-age reading alone. Any maintained attachment to John-1022 is an uncertain identification of the father, not an additional record and not evidence for Alexander’s parentage.


The distinction matters because the neighbouring tenancy pattern is tempting but not decisive. The 1834 tithe names Alexander and Robert Glasgow at Lisnagaver, while later valuation lots 24, 25 and 26 are associated with John, Alexander and Thomas under Robert Harvey. Acreage, field-book and adjacency arguments can suggest tenancy succession or a broader network. They cannot establish a biological descent, and Plantation-measure tithe acreage cannot be numerically matched to statute-measure valuation acreage to manufacture an inheritance. The 1836 field book names Robert Glasgow and Archibald McCaughan junior in the house section but does not name Alexander; its land section does not supply occupier names. It therefore cannot decide who lived together, who inherited, or whether Alexander was a brother of John or Thomas.


Thomas Glasgow-987 and Daniel Glasgow-3896 have a stronger relationship argument than Alexander has with either. Daniel’s 1871 will, indexed through the PRONI Wills Calendar<ref name="Evidence968b317eb1">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx PRONI Wills Calendar].</ref>, calls the late Thomas his brother and identifies Daniel Neely Glasgow as nephew; Daniel Neely’s 28 June 1888 marriage<ref name="Evidence47f7d35ebe">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1888/10763/5925382.pdf 28 June 1888 marriage].</ref> in turn names Thomas Glasgow, farmer, as his father. Those two records establish Daniel and Thomas as brothers. Thomas’s PRONI calendar administration<ref name="Evidence9c6dade023">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/WillsCalendar_IE/WillsSearch.aspx PRONI calendar administration].</ref> adds that the Lisnagaver farmer died 21 June 1870 and administration went to widow Mary Anne on 7 September. It was an intestate administration, not a will, and it names no parent, sibling or heir beyond the widow. It cannot be used to extend the proved brotherhood into a parentage for Alexander.


Alexander may be a brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel. Shared locality, associated land, church context and descendant testimony make that a worthwhile research model. No confirmed Y-DNA comparison with an independently documented Thomas or Daniel descendant is supplied in this case. None of those sources says that Alexander was their brother, so the three men are not a proved sibling set. The 2020 correspondence records the older Alexander-and-Rosanna belief, but provides no demonstrably independent parentage source: the correspondent said she ''believed'' Thomas’s parents were Alexander and Rosanna, separately wondered whether the user’s Alexander was Thomas’s brother, and supplied neither a record citation nor usable autosomal-match data. The later FamilySearch Pedigree Resource File entries derive from an Ancestry member tree and conflict even on Rosanna’s reported death day. They show the circulation of a tradition, not its verification.

==== James's family: a promising identification with an unresolved title problem ====


Eliza Jane and Mary are explicitly sisters and daughters of '''James the Prescott carpenter'''. Identifying that James with Robert's brother is a strong property-based hypothesis, because both daughters convey interests in the same two parcels to Samuel. It is not yet proved by an express kinship or inheritance clause. Each daughter's '''one-ninth''' interest is also recorded in the official abstract. Together they exceed the '''one-sixth''' collective share given to James's children in Robert's will. Earlier ownership, additional inherited interests or a record error must be examined before treating these as a simple distribution of that sixth. The fractions cannot responsibly supply a child count.


The '''1868 Alexander deed has now been inspected'''. C114, 25 March 1868<ref name="Evidence1f5003a1e5">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRC-Y C114, 25 March 1868].</ref>, DGS 008200420, image 120, pp.164–165, identifies '''Alexander Glasco of Rochester, Monroe County, New York, express agent, son of James Glasco formerly of Prescott, carpenter'''. Through attorney Macneil Clarke he conveys '''one eighteenth''' for '''$166.66''' to '''Mary Eno Glasgow, widow of the late Samuel Glasgow'''. The accompanying C113 power of attorney<ref name="Evidenceff75c70d0d">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRK-B accompanying C113 power of attorney].</ref> was made at Rochester on '''28 December 1867'''; both instruments were registered on '''18 August 1868'''. The abstract's August date is therefore registration, not the deed's execution date.

==== 1892 New York probate citation: Nancy Glasgow's next of kin ====

The most informative parentage evidence located so far is not an Irish record but a legal notice published in New York. On 14 January 1892 the Clinton County Surrogate issued a citation on the petition of Hiram Walworth to prove the will of '''[[Glasgow-4070|Nancy Glasgow]]''' of Plattsburgh, an unmarried Irish-born woman who had described herself in January 1889 as "about 68 years" old.<ref name="NancyWill1889">Clinton County, New York, Surrogate's Court, ''Records of wills, 1807–1902'', vol. Q, pp. 255–259, will of Nancy Glasgow of Plattsburgh dated 15 January 1889, admitted 9 May 1892; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYC4-66V?view=fullText FamilySearch image 159].</ref><ref name="NancyCitation1892">''The Plattsburgh Sentinel'' (Plattsburgh, New York), 26 February 1892, p. 6, legal notices, citation in the estate of Nancy Glasgow, deceased, dated 14 January 1892; [https://www.nyshistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=plts18920226-01.1.6 New York State Historic Newspapers].</ref> The notice addresses heirs, next of kin and legatees. Its reference to both real and personal estate matters: the old restriction on collateral representation in personal property cannot by itself determine every relative's standing in this proceeding.<ref name="DeVoe1905">''Matter of De Voe'', 107 A.D. 245 (N.Y. App. Div. 1905), discussion of pre-1898 personal-property representation and the different treatment of real property; [https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/appellate-division/1905/107-ad-245.html published judicial opinion]. This later case explains the distinction; it is not a decree concerning Nancy's family.</ref>

The citation names no brother or sister directly. It lists only children of named people: '''James G. Glasgow, Ann and Lizzie''', children of John Glasgow, late of "Baladonly" (Ballydonnelly, Rasharkin parish); '''James Glasgow, Mary and Ann''', children of Alexander Glasgow, formerly of Rasharkin; '''Mary Jane and Ann''', children of Robert Glasgow; the Dysart children of '''[[Glasglow-11|Jane (Glasgow) Dysart]]''' in Rasharkin, Ballymena, New Zealand and West Troy; '''David, James and Samuel Anderson of Gortahar''', identified through separate household records as sons of '''[[Glasgow-4071|Elizabeth (Glasgow) Anderson]]'''; and the unnamed children of '''Ann McClelland''' and '''Mary Thompson'''.<ref name="NancyCitation1892" /> Nancy's will independently calls Margaret (Dysart) Kennedy her niece and Robert Anderson her nephew,<ref name="NancyWill1889" /> and the Rasharkin Presbyterian register records both as children of Glasgow mothers — Jane Glascaw at Granagh and Betty Glascaw at Drumack.<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555" /> Together these records support a probable network of deceased sibling branches: John, Alexander, Robert, Jane, Elizabeth, Ann and Mary. Elizabeth is identified through the baptism and household records, not named as a parent in the notice. The list's completeness and each person's exact relationship remain to be checked in the underlying petition.

The Alexander of this citation is probably Alexander of Lisnagaver. His daughters' marriages of 1871 and 1876 each name Alexander Glasgow of Lisnagaver as father, his son James was baptised at Lisnagaver in 1843, and he died in May 1888 — "formerly of Rasharkin" in the citation's language. Nancy, born about 1820–21, was roughly ten years his junior: probable sisterhood fits these ages; daughterhood does not. He spent his last years at '''Gortahar''', where the citation places his sister Elizabeth's Anderson sons in 1892. His son [[Glasgow-938|Robert]] is not named. The proposed Scottish continuity and alleged survival to 1902 need original-record verification; this potential omission prevents treating completeness as already demonstrated.

The John of the citation is probably '''[[Glasgow-867|John Glasgow of Lisnagaver]]'''; Lizzie and the Ballydonnelly residence remain identity checks. His documented children were Ann (born 1848; married Bellingham in 1875, naming father John) and '''James Garvin Glasgow''' — the "James G." of the notice; the "Lizzie" of the notice is an otherwise unrecorded daughter (the Elizabeth Ann on the family memorial, died 1933, was James Garvin's widow).<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4" /> A John Glasgow of Lisnagaver died on 24 June 1885 with son James as informant, which agrees with "late of".<ref name="JohnDeath1885">General Register Office of Ireland, civil death return, Ballymoney superintendent registrar's district, Dirraw district, entry 2: John Glasgow, Lisnagaver, 24 June 1885; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1885/06280/4799372.pdf register image].</ref> John's original 1846 marriage return names his father as '''John Glasgow, farmer''', and the 1851 census makes Samuel Glasgow, born in County Londonderry about 1790, John's brother.<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4" /> If Alexander and John shared a father, that father would be John Glasgow, farmer. Probable siblinghood alone does not distinguish a shared father from a shared mother or more complex half relationships.

The same document tells against the alternatives. '''[[Glasgow-987|Thomas Glasgow]]''' of Lisnagaver, whom earlier research treated as Alexander's possible brother, died in 1870 leaving children who were adults at Lisnagaver in the 1880s; had he been Nancy's brother they would have been her next of kin, yet none is cited while nieces in New Zealand are. This omission weighs against a simple reconstruction only if expected inclusion and completeness are established. It does not exclude Thomas or his proved brother [[Glasgow-3896|Daniel]] as Alexander's brothers or collateral relatives: Alexander could also share a parent with Thomas without Thomas being Nancy's sibling. The tradition naming [[Glasgow-3904|an older Alexander]] and Rosanna concerns Thomas; its extension to Alexander of Lisnagaver remains unproved. Likewise no member of the Glenleslie family of [[Glasgow-1367|Robert Glasgow]] and Catherine, previously attached as Alexander's parents, appears among Nancy's next of kin; [[Glasgow-1049|Robert of Doonbought]]'s daughters were Catherine, Margaret, Maria, Netta and Jane, not the Mary Jane and Ann of the citation. The Robert of the citation is more likely the second Lisnagaver tithe occupier of 1834 — 35 acres entered immediately after Alexander's 29 — and perhaps the Robert Glasgow of Gortereghy in Griffith's Valuation who died in Ballymoney district in 1868 aged 71; his daughters have not yet been found.<ref name="Evidenceb707c32b1e" /><ref name="GriffithRasharkin">[https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/antrim/rasharkin.htm Griffith's Valuation, Rasharkin parish], Glasgow occupiers at Lisnagaver (Alexander, John, Thomas), Gortereghy (Daniel, Robert) and Dromore (James).</ref><ref name="Evidenced078ae5073" />

The reconstructed family of John Glasgow, farmer, runs from Samuel (about 1790, County Londonderry) through Robert (about 1797), John (about 1801, County Antrim), Jane (about 1804), Alexander (about 1811), Elizabeth (by about 1816), Ann and Mary, to Nancy (about 1820–21) — a span that warrants checking estimated ages, identities and possible multiple unions; it does not establish two marriages of a particular parent. If these identities and a shared household are correct, their different birth counties suggest a possible movement from County Londonderry to Rasharkin parish; the John Glasgow recorded as a Desertoghill flax grower in 1796 ([[Glasgow-4090|Glasgow-4090]]) is a plausible but unproved identity for the father, and John of Lisnagaver later married a Desertoghill woman at Garvagh. No record yet names Alexander's father in his own right, and the citation cannot distinguish full from half siblings. The decisive record is Nancy's underlying Clinton County probate petition, which should state each cited person's relationship to her.

=== The Larne connection: a working family reconstruction ===

'''The Larne–Kilwaughter family is a priority origin hypothesis for Alexander's paternal line.''' The useful model connects an Irish branch with a branch that moved to South Carolina in the 1770s. Identifying him with [[Glasgow-3905|Glasgow-3905]] means testing whether he was '''Adam of Inishrush's father''': 3905 represents that unidentified parental role, rather than a second man established by records. Its placeholder status neither supports nor disqualifies James.

==== Where the DNA and the wider catalogue narrow the search ====


The DNA evidence is positive family evidence. Alexander's established descendant line and James J's line share '''R-FT20271''', are three steps apart at Y-111 and share DYS714=27. Alongside James J's South Carolina origin and the documented Kilwaughter emigrant family, that makes the Larne connection worth pursuing ahead of an arbitrary same-surname pedigree. The American household evidence was not derived from the DNA, so their agreement is meaningful. But the proposed links from James J to Robert and Archibald are the very links being tested: they cannot also be counted as an independent proof that the match descends from Archibald.


There are already '''two additional historical comparison routes''' in the public project<ref name="Evidencedb3c53b8e9" />: a reported Robert-1143 line tested at Y-111, and a reported John-822 line tested at Y-67. They place the Larne and Inishrush questions within the same broader STR research network. Their public broad haplogroup labels do not yet establish either as FT20271-positive. Auditing those descent paths and obtaining resolved SNP states would test the proposed geographic connection more directly than treating all current FT20271 matches as interchangeable. John's omission of Alexander from his family Bible weakens '''John as Alexander's father''', not John as a collateral relative.


The proposed older Larne tree must also be tested. James-1509’s imported and live attachment is to [[Glasgow-1505|William-1505]], while the reviewed catalogue also carries a competing Hugh hypothesis. A William Glasgow, merchant of Larne, witnessed the 1760 lease; his identification with William-1505 needs checking against the other adult Williams. The derivative 1737 baptism names Hugh. [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh-1503's]] monument names a different adult son James, born about 1747/48. Both cannot casually be treated as the same child; identifying both as surviving sons of one Hugh would need explanation. William and Hugh's 1736 joint tenancy establishes association, while the proposed connections from them and Robert-1143 to [[Glasgow-1502|Robert-1502]] remain unproved. This is the unsettled joining generation, rather than a reason to disregard the well-supported branches below it.


A second origin model remains useful: the two '''Hugh Glasgow householders recorded in Tamlaght O'Crilly in 1740''', followed by a parish Hugh in 1772, could represent local continuity behind Adam. That pattern is not fully followed, and applying it to Adam-3902 depends on the unproved brotherhood. These are substantive local alternatives. They prevent treating a good Larne reconstruction as already the only surviving family.


'''The research can now be narrower:''' test Archibald's missing adult son in estate '''647'''; test the Larne household through William-3324's surviving '''1815 will, D300/1/5/49''', the '''1762 marriage''' and earlier Belfast records; identify Alexander's immediate family in '''CR5/32/1/1/1–2'''; and resolve the DNA placement of the specific Larne and Inishrush comparison lines. Each addresses a particular missing connection. The research priorities explain the outcomes to look for.

The 1861 deed<ref name="Evidence6e02c4a48a" /> now establishes the Canadian connection for Thomas and Daniel: their documented siblings include Robert and Samuel of Prescott, John the watchmaker, Mary Glasgow Black and brother James. === How the evidence supports this account ===

The account separates the '''recorded event''', '''the identification of its people''', and '''the conclusion drawn from it'''. A baptism can directly name a child’s parents while leaving the child’s later identity unknown. A death can have an exact date while remaining a probable match to Alexander. These are different questions and should carry different qualifications.

==== What an unsuccessful search means ====


Missing evidence is useful only when we know what should have been recorded and what survives. The unnamed 1838 child’s absence from all relevant parts of the household return has more bearing on a survival hypothesis than an unrestricted web search finding nothing. It still cannot establish a death date by itself. A gap in the baptism transcription, a register starting after the marriage, and an archive image requiring onsite access are three different limitations.


The research history records completed searches and the wider register of inaccessible originals and unresolved identities; the focused next tests appear below. The next work is prioritised by the proposition it could resolve, not by the number of databases left to search. No numerical parent score is treated as a probability or allowed to replace these source-based arguments.

=== New Dysart–Glascaw network lead ===

The Rasharkin baptism register records '''Jane Glascaw''', born 29 April 1846, as daughter of '''Thos Glascaw''' and '''Mary Ann McCrackin''' at Lisnagaver, and records later children of Jane and James Dysart in Granagh and Crushybracken. FamilySearch's indexed civil-registration entry records '''John McCaughan''' marrying '''Sarah Dysart''' at Rasharkin on 18 March 1851. The associated persons identify '''Jas McCaughan''' as John's father and '''Jas Dysart''' as Sarah's father. === FamilySearch identity collision: Scottish and Rasharkin Alexanders ===

The authenticated FamilySearch Tree profile [https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/details/G8WJ-HFW G8WJ-HFW] is internally conflated. Its source list contains Irish records for the Rasharkin Alexander, but its family panel also attaches a Scottish wife, Mary McCaughan (MQ57-B2Y), Scottish children and a Barony, Lanarkshire marriage. The archived discussion on this profile identifies the Scottish marriage as Alexander Glasgow and Mary Fleming on 12 June 1838 in Barony, Lanarkshire, with an 1841 Barony household headed by a flesher.

That Scottish couple is distinct from this profile's Rasharkin farmer: the latter's son James was baptized at Gortereagh on 9 February 1837, before the Scottish marriage, and Alexander appears with Mary and children at Lisnagaver in 1851. The Mary Fleming marriage is therefore not evidence against [[McCaughan-222|Mary McCaughan]]. The FamilySearch tree is useful for locating the conflict but is not proof of Mary's parents or of Alexander's parentage.

=== Pre-1790 Rasharkin McCaharan graveyard root ===

The [https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinCOI/graveyard.html Rasharkin Church of Ireland graveyard transcription] records '''Andrew McCaharan''', who died '''1 February 1738 aged 69''', and separately names his son '''John McCaharan''' on the same memorial. This is a direct local memorial and places the McCaharan spelling in Rasharkin more than a century before [[McCaughan-222|Mary Glasgow]]'s estimated birth.

It is a new root cluster for the surname study, but not a proved ancestor line: the transcription gives no John's wife, townland, full death information or intervening generations. It strengthens the case for a long-established local surname population while leaving Mary's parentage unproved. The original stone image or burial/register material should be sought to recover the remainder of John's inscription.

=== New full 1803 Ballintoy McCaughan household audit ===

The complete [https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1803traillcensus.pdf 1803 Ballintoy agricultural census] reveals several distinct early McCaughan households beyond the previously isolated Coulrasheskin entries:

* '''Broughgammon:''' deceased Dennis M'Caghan; widow Margaret McCurdy; John, Molly, Betty, Nancy and Matty.
* '''Drumnagessan/Cairn-Hill:''' John M'Caghan and Sarah McCaw; sons David, Archibald, John and James; daughter Isobel.
* '''Drumnagessan:''' Daniel M'Caghan and Rose McCurdy; daughters Catherine, Sally and Isobel.
* '''Templastragh:''' Daniel M'Caghan and Rose McCurdy; sons John, Alexander, Roger and Robert; daughter Mary.
* '''Templastragh:''' Hector M'Caghan and Peggy Laverty; son Zachariah and daughter Rose.
* '''Templastragh:''' John M'Caghan and Jane Sinclair; sons Hector and Daniel.
* '''Craige:''' Angus M'Caghan and Elizabeth Glass; sons Hugh and Archibald; daughter Belle.

The two Daniel-and-Rose entries occur as separate census households in different townlands and must not be merged without proof. The Templastragh Mary is directly recorded as a daughter of Daniel M'Caghan and Rose McCurdy, but no age, later marriage, migration or Rasharkin connection is supplied. This confirms a substantial early, multi-branch Ballintoy network, but none of these households can presently be assigned as the parents of [[McCaughan-222|Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow]]. Targeted WikiTree searches found no matching profiles for these exact household combinations, so no IDs are invented here.

=== 1824 Templastragh tithe continuity ===

The later [https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrimrevisionnamespdf.pdf North Antrim tithe revision] independently preserves the Templastragh cluster: it lists '''Zackariah McCahan''', '''Daniel McCahan''', '''Alexander McCahan''' and a '''widow McCahan''' there in 1824. Zackariah is especially notable because the 1803 Ballintoy census names '''Zachariah McCaghan''' as the son of '''Hector McCaghan''' and '''Peggy Laverty'''. Daniel and Alexander also recur as names in the 1803 Daniel-and-Rose household, although the tithe does not state their relationships or ages.<ref name="Evidence1824TemplastraghContinuity">[https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrimrevisionnamespdf.pdf North Antrim tithe revision names], records 800–801 and 807–814.</ref>

This is genuine chronological corroboration for a continuing McCaughan/McCahan presence in the same Ballintoy townland, and it helps distinguish the early Templastragh households from isolated name occurrences. It still cannot identify the 1803 Mary as the later [[McCaughan-222|Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow]]: the tithe gives no women’s identities beyond the widow, no marriages or children, and no movement toward Lisnagaver or Gortereghy.

=== 1766–1860 Templastragh locality trail ===

The 1766 [https://www.billmacafee.com/1766census/1766religiouscensusballintoy.pdf Religious Census for Ballintoy] records '''Daniel M'Kaughen''' in '''Templastragh''', with a household size of five. This is a direct pre-1790 occurrence of the same distinctive given name and townland later seen in the 1803 census. The 1803 household is much larger—Daniel M'Caghan, Rose McCurdy and five listed children, including Mary—and the 1824 tithe revision again lists Daniel McCahan in Templastragh.<ref name="Evidence1766TemplastraghDaniel">[https://www.billmacafee.com/1766census/1766religiouscensusballintoy.pdf 1766 Ballintoy Religious Census], record 348.</ref>

The later [https://www.irishgenealogyhub.com/antrim/griffiths-valuation/parish-of-ballintoy.php Griffith's Valuation index] also lists '''Daniel McCahan''' and '''Elizabeth McCaughan''' in Templastragh. Because the valuation is a later occupier index and does not state ages, spouses or parentage, this may represent a younger Daniel or a different household; it cannot be assumed to be the 1803 man. Taken together, the records establish a long-lived Daniel/McCaughan presence in Templastragh from 1766 through the mid-nineteenth century and justify targeted searches for a marriage or baptismal record connecting the households.

This materially strengthens the Ballintoy cluster but still does not prove that the 1803 Mary was [[McCaughan-222|Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow]] or that Daniel and Rose were her parents.

=== Later Daniel-and-Elizabeth Templastragh branch ===

An [https://www.ancestry.com/genealogy/records/jane-mccaughan-24-1mzn0 Ancestry public-name index] identifies '''Jane McCaughan''', born '''12 November 1834''' at '''Templastragh''', as daughter of '''Daniel McCaughan''' and '''Elizabeth Rogers'''; the same compiled entry estimates both parents at about 1800–1847 and says Jane later emigrated to New York. === First Kilraughts register: confirmed archival target ===

The [https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/accessions/2002/02digests/religion.htm National Archives catalogue] confirms that '''First Kilraughts Presbyterian Church''' records survive at PRONI as '''MIC/1P/462''', including registers and minute books from '''1815–1984'''. === Collateral Drumadarragh McCaughey branch ===

=== 1740–1796 Tamlaght O'Crilly / Drumcannon McCaughan continuity lead ===

The 1740 Protestant Householders' Returns identify '''John McCahan''' and '''James McCahan''' in '''Tamlaght O'Crilly''', in the Loughinsholin barony. This is an unusually early, exact-parish occurrence of two McCaughan-variant householders, decades before the Rasharkin baptismal material. The return gives no ages, household composition or relationship between the two men.<ref name="Evidence1740TamlaghtMcCahan">[https://adamsfamilydna.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/1740-Protestant-Returns-Londonderry-County-Ireland.pdf 1740 Protestant Householders' Returns], records 1171–1172.</ref>

A later circa-1800 rent-roll transcription records four McCaughan tenants in '''Drumcannon''' in '''1791''': '''Samuel''', '''Matthew''', '''William''' and '''John'''. The source explains that the undated entries are part of farm rental lists dating roughly 1796–1814, so the dated 1791 entries should be treated as a landlord record, not a census. The 1796 Flaxgrowers' List then records '''William M'Caughin''' in '''Tamlaght O'Crilly''' with three wheels/looms.<ref name="Evidence1791Rent1796Flax">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/misc/rentrolls.html circa-1800 Bann Valley rent-roll transcription], Drumcannon entries 182, 185, 197–198; [https://www.billmacafee.com/1796flaxgrowerslist/1796flaxgrowersderry.pdf 1796 Flaxgrowers' List], record 4754.</ref>

This is new pre-1811 evidence in the same broader parish region and strengthens the case for investigating Tamlaght O'Crilly, Drumcannon and Gortereghy together. It does not prove the parents of [[McCaughan-222|Mary Glasgow]]: the named tenants have no demonstrated relationship to her, and the 1791 William has not been shown to be the 1796 William. The next test is to trace these names through surviving estate papers, Presbyterian records and valuation revisions for a daughter Mary born about 1811 or a transfer into Lisnagaver/Gortereghy.

=== 1817 First Ballymoney McCaughan household: a new Mary-parent candidate ===

Rev. Robert Park's 1817 register of the First Ballymoney Presbyterian Church records '''John McCaughan [McCahon]''', wife '''Mary McCaughan [McCahon]''', and son '''James McCaughan [McCahon]''' at '''Drumard [Drumart]''', house 8. The same register records '''Grissel McCaughan [McCahan]''' and '''Hugh McCaughan [McCahan]''' in a Bendooragh household, showing the variant forms in the Ballymoney-area Presbyterian network at the period when Mary Glasgow would have been a child.<ref name="Evidence1817BallymoneyMcCaughan">[https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1817parkcensus.pdf 1817 First Ballymoney Presbyterian register], records 2912–2914 and 570–571.</ref>

A separate compiled Ballyverdagh account lists a Drumant church-member household as John and Mary McCahon, with son James and daughters Mary and Elizabeth. Since that detail is not present in the searchable Park register entry and the underlying membership source has not been inspected, it remains a secondary lead. If the two records refer to the same couple, their daughter Mary would be chronologically compatible with [[McCaughan-222|Mary Glasgow]]'s estimated birth about 1811; no marriage, migration, residence or Glasgow connection has been found.

This is currently the strongest new chronological candidate for a Mary-parent household outside the immediate Rasharkin cluster, but it is not proof. The decisive test is to identify the original Drumard/Drumant membership sheet and trace John and Mary McCaughan through Ballymoney Presbyterian baptisms, marriages and valuation records.<ref name="EvidenceDrumantMcCahon">[https://electricscotland.com/webclans/m/maceachain2.htm compiled Ballyverdagh account].</ref>

=== Complete 1817 Ballymoney-area McCaughan audit ===

The full searchable 1817 register contains at least five distinct McCaughan/McCahon placements: '''Charles and Elizabeth McCaughan''' at Balnamore, with children James, Samuel, John, Ann, Daniel and Elizabeth and an older Mary whose relationship is uncertain; '''Samuel and Martha McCaughan''' at Taghey, with sons John and James; '''John and Mary McCaughan''' at Drumard, with son James; '''Grissel McCaughan''' and '''Hugh McCaughan''' in a Bendooragh household headed by William McMaster; and '''Elizabeth McCaughan''' in a Currysiskan household headed by Widow Knox.<ref name="Evidence1817CompleteMcCaughanAudit">[https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1817parkcensus.pdf complete searchable 1817 register], records 1239–1248, 1383, 1436–1439, 2912–2914 and 570–571.</ref>

The separate compiled account's Drumant list of daughters Mary and Elizabeth may represent a different membership list, a different townland, or an expanded/parallel record, but it cannot currently prove that the Drumard couple had a daughter Mary. The Drumard family remains a possible chronological comparison branch, but its evidential weight is lower than the initial reading suggested.

The audit also identifies a Balnamore Mary McCaughan candidate, but the register marks her relationship as uncertain and suggests only that she may be Charles's mother. None of the five placements supplies a marriage, parent statement, migration record or Glasgow link. [[McCaughan-222|Mary Glasgow's]] parents therefore remain unproved.

=== Pre-1790 Ballintoy record: Archd. McKaughin at Lisbellanagroagh More ===

The 1766 Religious Census for Ballintoy parish records '''Archd. McKaughin''' at '''Lisbellanagroagh More''', identified as Protestant. It cannot identify this Archibald as her father, and Lisbellanagroagh More is not the same place as Lisnagaver/Gortereghy. === Lisbellanagroagh continuity: Catherine M'Caghan and Daniel McCaw ===

The 1803 Ballintoy census records '''Kath. M'Caghan''', standardised as Catherine McCaughan, at '''Lisbellanagroagh Beg'''. She was listed as the wife of John McIlfatrick and as Church of Ireland; the row gives her age as 29, implying an estimated birth about 1774. The 1824 Ballintoy tithe book then records '''Danl. McCaw''' at '''Lisbellanagroagh More''', the neighbouring “More” townland where the 1766 census had recorded Archd. McKaughin.

These records create a continuous locality trail from an Archibald in 1766, to a McCaughan woman in the adjoining townland in 1803, to a McCaw occupier in More in 1824. They do not prove that Catherine was Archibald's daughter, that Daniel was related to either person, or that this Cary cluster was the family of [[McCaughan-222|Mary McCaughan Glasgow]]. === FamilySearch record-hint collision: James McCaughan and Alexander McCaughan ===

The logged-in FamilySearch record search returned an indexed Ireland marriage result describing '''James Mc Caughan''' as father of '''Alexander Mc Caughan'''. The attached Family Tree match was '''MCGP-3S2''', but that profile is James McCaughan born about '''1827''', with spouse Catharine McConachie and children Alexander McCaughan ('''1847–1921''', 96QG-NVJ) and Robert Mc Caughan ('''1853–1934''', K4GP-RD8). The tree profile has no sources and the relationship was added in 2020.

This is a new and important exclusion. The attached tree person cannot be the older James proposed as Mary's father: he is too young, and his son Alexander was born decades after Mary's marriage and the 1837–1844 Glasgow baptisms. The indexed father statement may belong to a different McCaughan family or be an aggregation error; it must not be cited as evidence for Mary's parentage. == Biography ==
=== Alexander’s life in its local setting ===

Alexander’s records describe a family rooted in a small part of County Antrim, with children whose later lives lead beyond it. His clearest surviving household is at Lisnagaver in 1851: an Antrim-born farmer, his wife Mary, and three children. Earlier baptisms recover the beginnings of that family; later marriages and the Elder tenancy connect it to the next generation. The probable Gortahar death completes the broad outline, with the last identity link still open.



==== The places in his life ====


Gortereghy<ref name="Evidencec9d92bcd01">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin-upper/gortereghy/ Gortereghy].</ref>, written Gortereagh in the baptism transcription, adjoins Lisnagaver<ref name="Evidence7d988f87c8">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/lisnagaver/ Lisnagaver].</ref> to the south. Gortahar<ref name="Evidence10a9c7be48">[https://www.townlands.ie/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/gortahar/ Gortahar].</ref> lies northeast, beyond Moneyleck. They are distinct townlands within the same parish. The map shows approximate modern townland locations, not reconstructed houses or field boundaries.


Both spouses reported first marriage in 1836. Their children’s baptisms place them at Gortereagh in 1837–38 and Lisnagaver by 1843. That suggests a change in the family’s recorded residence between neighbouring townlands; it does not date a move precisely or establish a return to a paternal home. Mary’s possible local family connections deserve investigation in their own right.


The census’s farmer and literate household, the small assessed tenancy and the children’s marriages recover part of Alexander’s circumstances. Later records call him a labourer, and his son-in-law succeeds him on the holding. These changes are compatible with an altered working role as he aged, but their cause is unknown. No inspected source establishes eviction, poverty, or illness-induced retirement. The record sequence and farm analysis distinguish those observations from assumptions about his life.


The following account traces marriage and children, examines the surviving household, then follows the farm, probable death and paternal connections. Missing parentage is one question within that family history.



=== Marriage, Mary’s family and the children ===

Alexander Glasgow and Mary/Molly McCaughan are a documented couple. Their 1851 household reports first marriage in 1836, but no original marriage entry has been located. Rasharkin Presbyterian’s surviving marriage register begins in 1845; First Kilraughts material (Coleraine Family History Society film 197, marriages from 1831) remains a focused alternative.


The marriage-year statement fits the first directly located record sequence. The published transcription of the original Rasharkin Presbyterian register, PRONI MIC1P/292, records the same parental couple at Gortereagh: James Glascaw was born 17 January and baptised 9 February 1837 to Alex and Mary McAughin; an incomplete 1838 entry records a Glascow child of Alex and Molly McAughern; and a later James Glascow was born 9 October 1843 and baptised 7 January 1844 to Alex and Molly McAughern at Lisnagaver. The named transcription can be checked at Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms].</ref>. The register transcription preserves Mary/Molly and McAughin/McAughern. The repeated parental names and residences support their identification with Mary McCaughan while retaining the spellings actually recorded.


The Gortereagh residence is meaningful maternal context, but it is not a parentage proof. The 1834 tithe list includes William and James McCaheran there, a spelling compatible with the recorded McAughin/McAughern/McCaughan forms. This makes a McCaughan family connection a reasonable explanation to test for the newly married couple’s residence, perhaps through Mary's people or a subtenancy. It does not prove that either man was Mary's father, nor that the first son James was named for a maternal grandfather. The 1851 Lisnagaver evidence supplies a more concrete lead: Mary McCaheren, 22, lived with farmer Archibald McCaheren, 60, and Elizabeth in house 31. She is the strongest currently located candidate for the later 1855 bride who named her father as Archy, but that is a separate McCaughan problem. It does not establish Mary Glasgow’s parentage. Likewise, the household of widowed Sarah McCaghrin and grandchildren beside widowed Margaret Elder and children is evidence of a local network of families and neighbours, not an expressed kinship.


The Gortereagh names are recorded in the 1834 Rasharkin tithe book, PRONI '''FIN/5/A/236'''; the 1851 McCaheren and Elder groupings are in Lisnagaver houses 31 and 5. These are separate record observations, not confirmed maternal relatives. See the National Archives census collection<ref name="Evidence0b09d5bb14">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/ National Archives census collection].</ref> and PRONI tithe-book guide<ref name="Evidenceb39783b2e9">[https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/tithe-applotment-books PRONI tithe-book guide].</ref>.

An authenticated FamilySearch search adds a useful comparison lead: a John McCaughan marriage at Rasharkin on 18 March 1851 names '''Jas McCaughan''' as his father, while a separate 1836 Lisnagaver valuation entry names '''Archibald Mccaughan Junr'''. The same search returns Archey and John McCaheran in the 1822–1840 tithe collection. These entries strengthen the conclusion that several similarly named families occupied the area, but their original images and townlands still need checking; none currently proves Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceFamilySearchMcCaughan">[https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/record/results?count=100&q.anyPlace=Rasharkin&q.surname=McCaughan FamilySearch Rasharkin McCaughan search], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>

A separate public Geneanet tree repeats the John McCaughern–Sarah Dysart marriage and proposes a 1872 death for John and a daughter, Mary Anne Jane Rea McCaughern, at Crushybracken about 1858. This supplies a useful descendant-search route, but it is user-submitted derivative material and remains a collateral branch, not evidence for Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceGeneanetDysart">[https://pt.geneanet.org/fonds/individus/?go=1&niveaux_1___3869569569__=arbres&niveaux_2___3645179592__=arbres%23utilisateur&nom=MCCAUGHERN&sourcename__0__=bobspree Geneanet McCaughern public tree index], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>
